data.title: 2026 Mini John Cooper Works review: Uniquely fun, but one rival could spoil the party
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Every driver lining up on the Marina Bay grid for the Singapore Grand Prix cut his teeth in a go-kart, so I wonder what they would make (or their public-relations handlers would tell them to make of the Mini John Cooper Works (JCW).

After all, Mini insists that its cars are imbued with “go-kart feeling”, and the JCW is the purest expression of this idea.

It even has a Go-Kart mode, which sharpens the throttle response and adds heft to the steering, then puts power, torque and g-force readouts on the round central screen, in case you need a reminder that you’re having fun.

Karts are where racers learn their craft because they respond to every twitch of your wrist and, having no suspension, transmit every bump straight to your vertebrae.

Presumably, the original Mini was a bit like that, owing to its tiny size, wheel-at-each-corner layout and the fact that it rode on rubber cones instead of actual springs.

John Cooper, the English spannerman and racing driver, obviously saw something in the car, and his 1961 Mini Cooper was the result of a serious mechanical makeover.

He boosted a stock Mini’s power by more than half and fitted front disc brakes; Monte Carlo Rally wins followed in 1964, 1965 and 1967. His team also happened to win the Formula 1 constructors’ title in 1959 and 1960, so the John Cooper Works label means something.

On a Mini, it signals that a model sits one rung above the sporty Cooper S trim. The first factory-built JCW, launched in 2008, had reinforced pistons, a strengthened cylinder head and a bigger turbocharger, all borrowed from Mini’s racing programme at the time, all parts that a regular Cooper S didn’t get.

These days, JCW feels less like an engineering programme and more like a trim level. The current car even rides on touring tyres, which is like getting a sprinter to wear comfy loafers instead of running shoes.

Still, the new JCW might be the most fun car I’ve driven all year. It’s a heavy facelift of the last one rather than a clean-sheet design, sharing its platform and 2.0-litre turbo engine, though the cabin has been redone to match the latest Minis.

Power is unchanged at 231 horsepower, but torque rises from 320 Nm to 380 Nm, and a seven-speed dual-clutch gearbox replaces the old automatic.

It’s not all that fast by today’s standards, but I’ll be darned if the thing doesn’t feel alive. Lean on the throttle and it’s like you’ve angered the engine and exhaust, and even the car itself.

The wheel bucks in your hands from the ensuing surge of torque steer, and the hard suspension lets you know just why Mini people compare it to a go-kart.

The car’s raucous attitude extends to its styling flourishes, whether in the gloss-black grille or bonnet stripes, or the single fat tailpipe poking out of the middle of the rear diffuser, like a tongue stuck out at the cars behind.

The cabin is just as playful, with red stitching everywhere, racing-style bucket seats, a dashboard covered in knitted fabric, and a strip of red-and-black fabric on the steering wheel that looks like a tiny racing flag.

It makes for a delightful car, but there’s no getting away from the fact that it’s also a basic one. The tailgate is manual, cabin storage is scarce and the boot is tiny. Two adults will squeeze into the back with some cajoling, but they will resent you for it.

If high performance hijinks are your thing, the obvious alternative is the Volkswagen Golf GTI, which is more grown-up in terms of size and spirit. It’s a more comfortable and practical car, while the JCW is louder and cruder.

But the Mini is a thing of joy that continues to brighten the motoring world. It may be too late for me to start in karts and work my way up to a seat at Marina Bay, but driving the JCW could feel like the next best thing.

data.title: What real mental health support at work can look like
data.description:
WORLD Mental Health Day falls on Saturday (Oct 10). This year’s theme is “Lived Experiences Heard: Real Voices, Real Change”, which emphasises the importance of listening to people and urging changes in policy and the workplace.

Despite increased awareness of mental health in Singapore, a critical question remains: Have we achieved pervasive, actual implementation of real and tangible support for people with mental health conditions in our workplaces?

The honest answer is no.

Stigma continues to be real and present. Many who live with – or suspect they have – a mental health condition do not dare to voice what they are experiencing.

And many still do not seek help, fearing backlash, unspoken bias or being quietly sidelined in the office.

Surprisingly, or perhaps not, this hesitation is deeply ingrained in our work culture. It was evident even within my organisation, the Singapore Association for Mental Health.

In a closed-door consultation I held with colleagues shortly after stepping into the role of CEO, most indicated they were unsure whether to share that they have a condition.

Some were afraid of the potential repercussions of being seen simply attending a session on mental health with the CEO, wondering whether confidentiality would truly be kept.

This took place even though I had openly shared my personal lived experience at a staff town hall just months prior.

The takeaway was sobering. If employees inside an agency devoted entirely to psychiatric recovery still wrestle with the vulnerability of being seen having mental health conditions, the silence inside our wider commercial workplaces must undoubtedly be profound.

Rather than dictating policy from behind a closed boardroom door, we used our workplace to figure out what real, practical support looks like on the ground. I sent an open note inviting staff to sit down with me to co-develop these guidelines together.

At the first discussion, only a handful stepped forward. There was genuine apprehension in the room. Before we could even talk about policy, my priority was simply allaying fear, reassuring colleagues that it was safe to be present and their perspectives were essential.

I shared some thoughts on flexible work arrangements, and heard their questions and concerns first-hand.

By the second meeting, word had travelled that it was a safe space, and that leadership genuinely wanted a mental health framework co-developed. We had new joiners at the meetings.

This time, the discussions went straight into the real, thorny issues: How do we evaluate performance fairly? How do we prevent supervisor bias during appraisals? What practical handles do middle managers need so they do not panic, overstep or judge?

We have our third session coming up soon. For us, pace is the focus, not speed. Giving staff the space and time to reflect and align is key.

Facilitated co-development, coupled with genuine team ownership, will ultimately make internal policies, especially those related to sensitive and personal matters, work.

Three operational changes

The Workplace Fairness Act, which will protect employees from being discriminated against based on mental health conditions, is set to be enforced in 2027. With this, corporate Singapore can no longer rely on superficial wellness perks or passive hotlines to signal support.

Grounded in what we have learned from our own internal journey, we propose that companies need to move from intent to action in three distinct operational levels.

First, there must be genuine buy-in at the leadership level. Company leaders need to see that a compassionate culture is not a soft human-resources exercise, but a standard staff-retention and sustained-performance strategy.

Top-level backing is necessary to establish clear procedural protection, such as a confidential safe-disclosure pathway in which an employee can request temporary adjustments, with the assurance that performance will be judged on output rather than face time, and that their career mobility will not be jeopardised.

Second, HR professionals need to establish structured, phased return-to-work protocols.

Consider a simple reality check: If an employee breaks a leg, they go to a doctor, take medical leave and return to daily activity gradually, as the leg heals. You would never expect them to run a marathon on their first day back at work.

A severe mental health condition warrants the exact same operational logic. Expecting someone recovering from clinical depression or severe burnout to jump straight back into an intense 45-hour workweek invites immediate relapse.

A practical return-to-work framework means maintaining light-touch contact during medical leave to agree on what colleagues are told regarding health accommodations, returning to work with reduced hours or lighter duties, and holding regular review check-ins to calibrate workloads before ramping up to, and resuming, full responsibilities.

Lastly, front-line supervisors and managers must be equipped with practical handles. This, I believe, will be the toughest part for most organisations.

Managers do not need to become counsellors or clinicians. Expecting them to diagnose or provide therapy is unrealistic and counterproductive.

What they need is the training and confidence to put across that performance remains the key assessment metric, while maintaining empathy and fairness in their reviews.

That means learning to spot early behavioural shifts, asking constructive workload-focused check-in questions and having clear referral boundaries, so they can connect struggling staff to professional support without awkwardness or fear.

Ultimately, moving from policy to practice will transform workplace well-being. Side effects from medication and the day-to-day realities of our conditions do not make us any less responsible; they are standard challenges along a recovery curve.

We all want to engage in meaningful, dignified work and be contributing members of the team.

When employees know their employer offers tangible structures to navigate human vulnerability, they are motivated to give their best. Slowly, stigma will be reduced, and hopefully, eliminated.

The writer is CEO of the Singapore Association for Mental Health

data.title: Issue 215: Coalâs role in South-east Asian energy security; Singaporeâs electricity import woes
data.description:
Energy transition

Beware the overly narrow view of energy security

The reframing of the renewable energy transition as a matter of security instead of a climate priority has been a mixed bag for climate action.

On one hand, the security impetus has fuelled a desire among many countries to diversify away from oil and gas towards more renewable sources of energy. However, the pursuit of energy security has also rekindled the lifespan for coal, especially in countries like Indonesia or Vietnam where domestic coal resources exist.

An important lesson lies beneath that dynamic: The energy transition cannot be tackled as a one-dimensional problem, or it will fall short. Just as the climate change movement has learnt that the energy transition cannot happen at the expense of energy resilience and security, the pursuit of secure energy must be undertaken with the understanding that global warming is ultimately destabilising. Coal and fossil fuel policies should not close a window but leave the door open.

That dissonance between the climate-first and security-first approaches in the energy transition is apparent in the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) Asean Energy Security Review, which projects that while renewables will capture a larger share of electricity generation in South-east Asia in the next five years, coal and gas generation will continue to grow as well.

The review’s projections trace from a fundamental expectation of growing energy needs in the region. For instance, electricity demand in South-east Asia is expected to grow at an average of 5.4 per cent every year from 2026 to 2030 on the back of growing demand for cooling, data centres and industry.

The security question as addressed by the review is how to “ensure the uninterrupted availability of energy at affordable prices, while maintaining the flexibility and resilience needed to manage shocks and longer-term stresses”.

The review’s recommendations are centred on three key strategies: Diversify energy supply sources and routes, make greater use of domestically available energy resources, and accelerate electrification alongside efficiency improvements.

Renewables tick many boxes. For example, the review describes South-east Asia’s solar supply chain self-sufficiency as “among the world’s most secure” with existing manufacturing capacity able to supply projected regional demand across solar modules, cells and wafers.

Looking ahead, the review expects wind generation in South-east Asia to grow by about 26 per cent annually from 2026 to 2030, while solar generation could grow by about 23 per cent a year over the same period. Together, solar and wind’s share of the region’s electricity mix will increase to 11 per cent by 2030 from about 5 per cent in 2025.

The security challenge for greater adoption of renewables in the region has less to do with generation capacity and more with improving grid and storage infrastructure to handle the inherent variability of solar and wind generation.

But renewables are not the only source of energy that is growing. The review projects that coal demand in the region will grow by about 4.4 per cent annually through 2030, the fastest pace globally. Indonesia, the world’s largest coal exporter, accounts for more than 56 per cent of the growth, with Vietnam and the Philippines also growing coal generation in the coming years.

The reason is simple: Self-reliance is the key to energy security. If you’re a coal-producing country like Indonesia or Vietnam, the logical thing to do for energy security is to continue to use coal.

Coal is also a cheap and energy-dense fuel. The widespread use of captive coal plants – off-grid coal generators – for industrial uses in Indonesia also makes coal difficult to replace without significant costs to communities and economies.

“Indonesia has committed to reach net zero by 2060 or earlier,” the review notes. “This presents some challenges as coal is expected to remain important for both the power and industrial sectors, particularly for nickel processing. Coal is also an important provider of jobs, as well as state revenues through taxes and royalties. Some regions in Indonesia, such as East and South Kalimantan, are among the most coal-dependent regions in the world.”

Nevertheless, the review highlights the risks of continued dependence on coal without plans to transition to greener alternatives.

For example, continued reliance on captive coal in nickel production “may raise future transition costs, complicate net zero pathways and create export risks if importing Asean member states apply stricter sustainability standards to nickel supply chains”.

There is a danger in taking too narrow a view when framing the energy transition as a security issue.

There is no doubt that sufficient and reliable energy is essential for countries, especially in fast-growing South-east Asia. But policymakers and businesses must take a more holistic approach to energy security.

First, policies need to consider long-term security alongside short-term needs. Coal and natural gas may keep the lights on for now, but are these solutions that would still make sense a few decades from now?

Second, climate change needs to be recognised as a security concern as well. The planet-scale impact of climate change – weather catastrophes and agricultural losses, for instance – has the potential to cause tremendous disruptions to social and economic systems. Lights at night are important, but so is food at mealtimes. The impact is also widespread across many vectors – for example, higher temperatures can reduce the efficiency of solar panels.

The shift in the energy transition conversation to one dominated by energy security has helped to highlight the benefits of renewable energy beyond being greener. But it is important to ensure that the new paradigm does not devolve into short-sighted actions concerned only with geopolitics. Just because a war in the Middle East is highly consequential at the moment does not mean that climate change has lessened or that climate needs are no longer pressing.

Energy transition

Time to sharpen Singapore’s energy transition strategy

It seems increasingly likely that Singapore will miss its interim climate goals as a major energy import strategy struggles to progress quickly enough.

Singapore is likely to miss its target of importing about 6 gigawatts (GW) of low-carbon electricity by 2035, says research firm Wood Mackenzie. As a result, green electricity imports will probably account for only about 15 per cent of the electricity mix by 2035, about half of the targeted one-third contribution.

Wood Mackenzie’s projection is based on the fact that although Singapore has approved 9.25 GW of import projects, none of that capacity has begun construction. The analysis identifies a few key hurdles that hold back progress: “Export permit frameworks, project bankability, cross-border transmission financing, and the lack of a complete market mechanism that allows Singapore buyers to claim the carbon value of imported electricity.”

The challenge for Singapore is that none of these hurdles are fully within its control. For example, Wood Mackenzie notes that Vietnam still has no legal mechanism for a foreign developer to develop generation and to export it through a dedicated undersea cable. Cambodia lacks an export regulatory framework and surplus generation, with blackouts a regular occurrence. The firm does not expect exports from either country by 2035.

Singapore has pledged, under the terms of the Paris climate agreement, to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 60 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (MtCO2e) by 2030 after peaking earlier. By 2035, the country aims to reduce emissions further to between 45 and 50 MtCO2e.

Singapore’s emissions remain on an upward trajectory. Singapore reported national emissions of 55.5 MtCO2e for 2023. The country’s total electricity generation in 2023 was 57.4 terawatt hours (TWh). In 2025, generation increased about 5 per cent to 60.4 TWh. Singapore’s grid emissions factor declined only about half of that between 2023 and 2024.

Electricity demand is also growing faster than initially expected. In a September call for bids to develop additional gas-fired generation by 2031 and 2032, the Energy Market Authority revised its earlier outlook for peak demand. The official projection is now for peak demand to increase at a compound annual growth rate of 2.9 to 6.5 per cent from 2025 to 2034, higher than the initial forecast of 2.4 to 4.8 per cent.

Singapore will probably have to revise its climate targets to better align them with current circumstances, but the more important task is to review the climate strategy to find ways to hasten progress on the country’s energy transition.

Energy imports seem unavoidable for resource-starved Singapore, so Singapore needs to sharpen its plan to overcome the hurdles to progress. Those hurdles were not all apparent when Singapore’s Energy 2050 Committee first formalised imports as a key pillar of the energy transition in 2022, but now they are. Reviewing the climate goals present an opportunity to be more focused about addressing these roadblocks.

The green-alternatives pillar can also be better focused on pathways that are more promising. Green hydrogen may not be as likely as once thought with viable scale still elusive. Nuclear looks increasingly like the most feasible way to lower domestic generation emissions. The geothermal pathway is still very nascent, but it could be worth accelerating research so that its feasibility can be determined sooner.

data.title: Delta Air cuts profit forecast as US$6 billion fuel-cost surge outweighs fare gains
data.description:
[CHICAGO] Delta Air Lines cut its annual profit forecast by nearly a quarter on Friday (Oct 9), as surging fuel costs, expected to add US$6 billion to its bill in 2026, overwhelmed resilient travel demand and higher ticket prices.

Its shares fell 3.5 per cent in premarket trading after the carrier cut its 2026 profit forecast for the first time this year and lifted its projected fuel-cost increase by US$2 billion as the Iran war has driven jet fuel prices sharply higher worldwide.

With no end to the war in sight, carriers are confronting their worst crisis since the pandemic.

The downgrade underscores a growing challenge for the industry: whether passengers will absorb further fare increases if fuel prices remain elevated. Airlines have already raised fares substantially this year, and analysts warn further increases could test travellers’ willingness to keep spending.

Delta, the first major global carrier to report third-quarter results, said fuel expenses for the period rose 62 per cent from a year earlier to US$4.1 billion, exceeding its July forecast by more than US$500 million.

“All of it’s fuel,” Delta chief financial officer Erik Snell told reporters when asked what drove the forecast cut, citing increases in both crude oil and refined jet fuel prices since the summer.

Delta now expects adjusted annual earnings of US$5.10 to US$5.60 a share, down from the US$6.50 to US$7.50 it forecast in July. The new midpoint of US$5.35 is below analysts’ average estimate of US$5.46, according to LSEG. It forecast US$4.5 billion in adjusted pre-tax profit for 2026.

Third-quarter adjusted earnings of US$1.72 a share narrowly missed analysts’ average estimate of US$1.76, according to LSEG. Its adjusted operating margin fell to 9.4 per cent from 11.1 per cent.

Rivals United Airlines, American Airlines and Southwest Airlines are due to report later this month. Ryanair Group CEO Michael O’Leary warned on Thursday that European airlines could face more than another year of elevated fuel costs due to the war.

Higher fares

US airlines spent US$42.9 billion on fuel for scheduled flights in the first eight months of 2026, nearly US$13.2 billion more than a year earlier, despite using slightly less fuel, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics.

Strong demand and limited growth in seats have helped carriers pass higher fuel costs on to passengers. US airline fares rose an average of about 25 per cent from a year earlier in the five months through August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ consumer price index.

With fuel prices remaining elevated and planned industry capacity growth set to accelerate in the fourth quarter from the third, analysts are watching whether carriers, including Delta, can raise fares further without discouraging travel.

Deutsche Bank analysts expect the industry to recover a smaller share of higher fuel costs through revenue measures in the fourth quarter, with full recovery not expected until early 2027.

Delta said demand remains strong. With almost 60 per cent of the fourth quarter already booked, it expects revenue growth of about 20 per cent from a year ago, Snell said.

“The general sentiment from our experts is that much of the revenue results and outlooks are held up by the premium passenger and higher fares,” Third Bridge analyst Liam Dorsey said.

“At the moment, those higher prices have not destroyed any demand and it remains to be seen how long that will last.”

Refinery advantage

Delta has an advantage over other major US airlines: its ownership of a refinery outside Philadelphia that Snell expects to generate US$700 million in profit this year.

“We have a refinery that gives us an offset, a partial offset to fuel prices that no one else does,” he said.

Bought in 2012, the Monroe refinery processes crude oil into jet fuel and other products. Delta still pays market prices for fuel transferred to its airline operations, but retains the refining profit within the company.

That helps when the gap between crude and refined fuel prices widens, increasing costs for airlines buying from outside suppliers. The protection varies with refining margins, however, and the refinery can lose money when those margins weaken.

But the refinery can only partly cushion the impact of higher fuel prices. Even with a projected refinery benefit of 40 cents a gallon, Delta expects its fuel cost to rise to US$4.25 a gallon in the fourth quarter from US$3.61 in the third.

Snell said fuel costs were expected to stay elevated for some time.

“Ultimately, fuel will come down. When that is, we’re not exactly sure,” he said. REUTERS

data.title: Haze task force convened, introduces measures as PSI hits the highest in 2026
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] N95 masks will be distributed to eligible Singaporeans who may be more vulnerable to the effects of haze or who may have limited means of obtaining them when air quality hits ‘very unhealthy’ levels, the authorities said on Friday (Oct 9).

Such levels are denoted by a Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) reading between 201 and 300.

Mask vending machines will also be made available at selected public transport hubs and social services offices to supplement the distribution efforts by grassroots organisations, Singapore’s haze task force announced in an update on Friday.

The task force is chaired by the National Environment Agency (NEA). Other agencies involved in the 28-member task force include the Ministry of Education, Sport Singapore, the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Health.

The update comes as the 24-hour PSI hit 192 in central Singapore at 6 pm, the highest so far in 2026, while the hourly PM2.5 reading stood in the “elevated” band at 123 in the central region.

Based on the current situation, it is possible that the PSI may exceed 200 and enter the “very unhealthy” range, the authorities said in a media statement issued at about 7 pm.

The task force last issued an update on Sept 4, when air quality in Singapore breached unhealthy levels for the first time since October 2023.

Eligible Singaporeans can collect N95 masks at vending machines at selected public transport hubs, Social Service Offices and PA venues using their NRICs. They may also ask a family member or friend to collect the masks on their behalf using the eligible person’s NRIC.

The task force added that there are sufficient stocks of N95 masks in retailers’ warehouses and government stockpiles and that it works closely with retailers to ensure the availability of N95 masks to the public.

When air quality breaches the “very unhealthy” threshold, air-conditioned rooms in community clubs, and selected Residents’ Committee and Residents’ Network Centres, will also be set up as haze shelters for the public to seek respite in.

If the PSI crosses into the ‘hazardous’ range when it exceeds 300, the opening hours of the haze shelters in the CCs will be extended to 10 pm.

The authorities said that while classroom lessons will continue, they may be modified as appropriate. For instance, students may be assigned work confined to a sit-down classroom setting and outdoor activities will be avoided.

The Education Ministry will only consider closing schools when air quality worsens further, when the forecast for the next day’s air quality is considered hazardous, when PSI levels are above 300.

The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) also reminded employers not to compromise on the health and safety of their employees, especially those involved in outdoor work.

When air quality is in the “very unhealthy” range, outdoor work for employees with chronic heart and lung conditions should be avoided. Outdoor work for vulnerable workers, especially the elderly and pregnant women, should be minimised.

If an employer still requires an employee to work due to extenuating circumstances, the employer is strongly urged to provide suitable masks like N95 masks, the task force said.

MOM also advised platform workers who are exposed to the haze while performing outdoor deliveries to follow the measures outlined in the advisory as much as possible.

Healthcare institutions such as public hospitals, polyclinics, and nursing homes have also activated haze preparedness measures, according to the task force. These include using air purifiers, closing the windows in the wards and corridors, and reducing ambient temperature through portable air coolers, where appropriate.

Community care providers offering residential and centre-based services have also been reminded to replace outdoor activities with indoor ones given the worsening air quality. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: Stocks to watch: SIA, CapitaLand Investment
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Oct 8):

SIA : Singapore Airlines and Air India will offer standalone code-share flights and “enhanced” frequent-flyer benefits, giving passengers “greater flexibility” in trip planning with 126 weekly flights, the two carriers announced on Wednesday. The expanded offerings cover flights between Singapore and eight Indian cities: Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Delhi, Hyderabad, Kochi, Kolkata and Mumbai. Shares of SIA ended at S$6.68 on Wednesday, S$0.02 or 0.3 per cent lower.

CapitaLand Investment : CapitaLand Investment and IOI Properties Group are now in exclusive due diligence for the acquisition of One Raffles Place, with a 50-50 joint bid submitted to owners OUE Reit and UOB, IOI Properties Group CEO Lee Yeow Seng told The Business Times on Wednesday. The offer was made about three months ago. Shares of CapitaLand Investment ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.04 higher at S$2.49 on Wednesday.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Frasers Property, StarHub, NTT DC Reit
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Oct 9):

Frasers Property : The CEO of Frasers Hospitality Eu Chin Fen will be stepping down, effective Jan 1, 2027. This follows the privatisation of Frasers Hospitality Trust and its portfolio optimisation. Frasers Hospitality’s leadership structure “will be strategically segmented, aligning with group resources, and reporting into senior group leadership”. Its chief operating officer Chew Hang Song will report to the group CEO. The counter closed at S$0.955 on Thursday, down S$0.01 or 1 per cent.

StarHub : The telco said it will acquire MyRepublic’s mobile business by Apr 30, 2027. The value of the transaction is not fixed, but is dependent on the total 4G and 5G MyRepublic mobile subscribers, average revenue per user of active 4G and 5G subscribers, as well as subscriber lifetime. StarHub will also pay additional cash amounts when specific subscriber migration milestones are met. Shares of StarHub ended at S$1.10 on Thursday, S$0.02 or 1.8 per cent lower.

NTT DC Reit : The real estate investment trust’s (Reit) manager is proposing changes to its management fee structure, that it expects will better align with the interests of the unitholders of the Reit. It is looking to link its performance fee directly to year-on-year growth in the distribution per unit. Units of NTT DC Reit ended 0.5 per cent or US$0.005 lower at US$0.935 on Thursday.

data.title: Dogged interest: Corporate buyers unleashed on animal health market
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Keep his clinic independent or join a corporate network? Veteran veterinary surgeon Ryan Leong had already faced this decision once before.

In 2024, the four-clinic chain Pets Avenue, which had begun with a single branch co-founded by Dr Leong in 2015, was sold by his business partner to American pet-care giant Mars.

In November, Mars came back with an interest in Pets Avenue Veterinary Clinic and Referrals, a clinic and surgical referrals practice that Dr Leong had set up in Telok Kurau earlier that year.

He admits that, as the clock ticked down to the August 2026 deadline for a response, the offer looked tempting.

“The carrot that was dangled before me was very attractive,” he says, without specifying the sum involved.

Ultimately, Dr Leong said “no”. He wanted the autonomy to build a like-minded team and make business decisions without involving a corporate owner with different priorities.

He has since rebranded his clinic as Chiron Veterinary Referrals, as the Pet Avenue name now belongs to Mars.

Still, his dilemma is one that more of Singapore’s independent vets may soon face, as corporate groups and private equity (PE) firms look to buy up clinics here.

Furry flurry

Vets and industry watchers to whom The Business Times spoke say the sector has become increasingly attractive to investors, as owners are willing to spend more on specialist care, while a fragmented market of small practices means that there are plenty of acquisition targets.

Based on checks by BT, Singapore had 125 veterinary clinics as at July 2026, of which roughly 80 per cent were independently owned.

Mars, the American chocolate and confectionery behemoth that also owns pet-food brand Royal Canin, has rapidly become the largest owner of clinics here through Mars Veterinary Health.

The conglomerate entered Singapore in 2020 with the purchase of Veterinary Emergency & Specialty (VES) Hospital in Whitley Road for an unspecified amount.

In April 2026, Workers’ Party MP Kenneth Tiong noted that Mars was running at least 19 of Singapore’s licensed veterinary centres, or about one-sixth of the market, at the time.

Other smaller corporate owners are also actively acquiring.

VetPartners – which is the largest vet group in Australia and New Zealand, with more than 260 clinics – bought Companion Animal Surgery in Balestier in 2019, its only clinic in Singapore.

Pet Space, which is Hong Kong’s largest vet group with 11 clinics there, bought Animal Recovery Veterinary Centre in Singapore and relaunched the formerly independent clinic under its own branding in January 2021.

Meanwhile, Catalist-listed Asia Vets Holdings was a cash company formerly known as Smartflex Holdings until it bought the Animal Ark brand in 2018. It now runs two clinics, in Springleaf and Tampines.

Fragmented market

The market activity does not surprise Dr Teo Boon Han, president of the Singapore Veterinary Association (SVA).

The interest from investors follows market trends in human healthcare here, he says, and is part of a broader global push towards consolidation in veterinary care.

The veterinary market attracts investors because of the size of the consumer dollar, as well as the prevalence of acquisition targets.

“Pet owners are increasingly willing and able to spend on preventive healthcare, diagnostics, and treatment for their fur kids,” adds Dr Teo, who is also managing partner of VetTrust Singapore and a senior veterinarian at Canopy Veterinary Centre in Jurong.

Singapore’s pet-care market is expected to reach US$184.4 million this year, up 3.5 per cent from 2025, according to Euromonitor International.

Spending on animal health is also shifting from routine vaccinations alone to more expensive services such as diagnostics, cancer care, complex surgery and intensive care, points out Sunny Soh, senior professional officer at the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT).

For PE firms, the draw goes beyond individual clinics.

“The real attraction is not veterinary clinics themselves,” says Luke Pais, EY-Parthenon’s Asean private equity leader, who has consulting experience in the pet-food sector.

“Once a network reaches scale, it becomes difficult to replicate because the moat is the ecosystem of vets, specialists, data, referral pathways and client relationships.”

Larger groups aiming for economies of scale in procurement, technology, marketing and administration can snap up clinics in a market that Dr Teo observes is highly fragmented. Most practices are either founder-run or part of brands with just two to five outlets.

Soh notes that a group that owns both neighbourhood clinics and a referral hospital can capture consumers across the whole patient journey – and, because most owners pay out of pocket rather than through insurers, providers have more freedom over pricing.

Unlike in Malaysia, where the government rejects veterinary practices that are set up as a partnership or company with shareholders who are not vets, anyone can own a clinic in Singapore as long as the vets working there are licensed.

Moreover, multinational groups can easily bring foreign vets into Singapore, says Dr Teo, since the working language here is English and accredited qualifications from the UK, US, Australia and New Zealand are accepted without requirements for further exams.

Staying independent

Many vets at independent practices value their nimble culture and lighter bureaucracy.

Specialist surgeon Patrick Maguire and his wife, Dr Rina Maguire, co-own Beecroft Animal Specialist and Emergency Hospital, a 24-hour referral hospital with around 150 staff and no outside investors.

Dr Patrick Maguire says he has been approached by corporate and PE buyers to sell, but talks never got far as he was not comfortable with the business structures proposed.

Like Dr Leong, he values being able to make decisions without “another layer of corporate ownership above us setting those priorities”.

Still, neither Dr Leong nor Dr Patrick Maguire thinks corporate ownership is inherently flawed.

SVA’s Dr Teo cites greater purchasing power, stronger recruitment, centralised administration and certain career opportunities as clear advantages that larger groups have over small practices.

SIT’s Soh estimates corporate-owned practices can leverage their scale to cut the unit costs of drugs and consumables by 15 to 30 per cent, while groups with pet-food arms can also capture value from prescription diets.

Yet the cost savings available to larger businesses do not automatically mean lower prices for pet owners, as they may be kept as margin, used to pay down acquisition debt or buy equipment.

As a result, some pet owners may be tempted to blame corporate ownership for rising bills and falling standards. Still, the independent vets who spoke to BT disagreed.

Dr Leong takes such complaints “with a pinch of salt”. When a clinic changes hands, the same vets and nurses usually stay on, he says.

As for one concern raised by EY-Parthenon’s Pais – that a network could steer referrals towards its own affiliated referral centres or laboratories – Dr Leong says that has not been his experience. Despite declining to join Mars, he still receives referrals from Mars-owned clinics “all the time”.

Dr Patrick Maguire, who previously worked in a corporate-owned practice in Ang Mo Kio for two years, adds that surgeons want good outcomes for their patients regardless of where they are based. The higher costs, he argues, are more because owners’ expectations have risen.

“You can’t have cut-price veterinary medicine and at the same time expect the highest levels of specialist care and 24-hour staffing.”

Watching the watchdogs

Overseas markets have seen significant consolidation.

Mars, the same privately held group buying up clinics here, paid US$9.1 billion for US hospital chain VCA Animal Hospitals in 2017. Other veterinary chains in its portfolio of more than 2,000 clinics include Banfield Pet Hospital, BluePearl and Linnaeus.

PE-backed groups have been busy too.

National Veterinary Associates, the largest private free-standing veterinary hospital chain in America, has been majority-owned since 2019 by a conglomerate with stakes in various global F&B and consumer brands.

The buyer, JAB Consumer Partners, also acquired Sage Veterinary Partners for US$1.1 billion and Ethos Veterinary Health for US$1.65 billion in 2022.

Meanwhile, VetPartners privatised Australia-listed National Veterinary Care in 2020 and was in turn bought out by Swedish investor EQT for A$1.4 billion (US$970 million) in 2023.

As deals piled up, competition in these markets thinned – prompting regulators to step in.

The US Federal Trade Commission warned that Mars’ VCA deal would likely raise prices and lower the quality of some speciality and emergency care. It made Mars sell 12 clinics and required JAB to offload clinics.

Australia’s competition regulator began requiring merger notifications in January 2026 and has referred at least one vet clinic acquisition for an in-depth review.

In the UK, where large groups own about six in 10 practices, the competition regulator found in March that prices had risen at twice the rate of inflation, with large groups charging 18.3 per cent more than independents. New rules introduced in response will require practices to publish prices and disclose their shareholders.

In Singapore, where investor interest in the vet industry is still nascent, the Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore (CCS) has not conducted any in-depth review of the level of competition in the sector or started any investigation, as it has not found reasons to suspect violations of the Competition Act at this point.

The agency actively monitors mergers and is aware that there have been acquisitions in the veterinary sector over the years, but has not received any notifications on them.

CCS remains open to looking into anti-competitive practices, such as collusion, abuse of dominant positions or mergers that might substantially lessen competition, and “will continue to monitor the market and review whether intervention may be necessary”, says its spokesperson.

EY-Parthenon’s Pais notes: “Singapore’s competition framework already prohibits mergers that substantially lessen competition.

“Consolidation is beneficial when scale funds better clinical care and productivity. It becomes problematic when the principal value driver shifts from efficiency to reduced customer choice and pricing power.”

For instance, the line is crossed when ownership is unclear, referrals are effectively captive or prices become difficult to compare, he adds.

If any regulation of veterinary market competition were to be introduced in Singapore, Dr Lee Yen Teik, senior lecturer in finance at the National University of Singapore Business School, expects that the authorities would require transparency, such as clear ownership disclosures and published prices, rather than impose curbs on ownership.

Buyers press “paws”?

Several years into the vet clinic buyouts, whether the acquisition activity is slowing down is an open question.

SIT’s Soh sees limits to further consolidation. In his view, Mars has already bought the “trophy assets”, leaving smaller targets that yield diminishing returns per deal.

BT has found no public record of acquisitions by Mars since it picked up Pets Avenue in 2024. The company did not respond to media queries.

Meanwhile, a spokesperson for Asia Vets tells BT that the company will stay disciplined as a buyer – weighing factors such as whether a clinic is “culturally compatible” with the group and can retain its vets, “rather than pursuing acquisitions simply to increase our scale”.

As for whether Asia Vets would consider a sale if approached by a corporate group or PE firm, the spokesperson says: “As with any listed company, the board would consider any proposal presented to it in accordance with its responsibilities and applicable regulations.”

The speed at which clinic networks can grow is limited by the local vet shortage, according to Soh. He expects corporate ownership to plateau at around 35 to 50 per cent of the market, leaving one dominant group, one or two smaller ones and a lasting independent fringe.

Independents with strong reputations or specialised capabilities will always have room, says SVA’s Dr Teo, adding that there are natural constraints on consolidation because Singapore is a small concentrated market.

He also notes that potential buyers can be very diverse – ranging from large, family-owned companies such as Mars with a long track record in veterinary care, to PE players with shorter investment holding periods that aim to sell within a few years.

What matters are safeguards to ensure fair competition and clinical independence, he adds. “While profits are important, I do hope that investors in the sector operate responsibly and respectfully, take care of the veterinary team on the ground, and serve as enablers to advance the veterinary profession.”

data.title: USÂ stocksÂ open higher as oil slips;Â telecoms hitÂ by SpaceX spectrum deal
data.description:
WALL Street’s main indexes opened higher on Friday (Oct 9) as oil prices retreated on easing Middle East supply concerns, though telecom shares remained under pressure after SpaceX’s spectrum acquisition raised competitive concerns across the sector.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 67.32 points, or 0.13 per cent, at the open to 51,298.96. The S&P 500 rose 22.35 points, or 0.29 per cent, to 7,787.71, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 149.59 points, or 0.55 per cent, to 27,342.93. REUTERS
